Ritu, you're filling in the course feedback form? Let me tell you about a form I filled in when I was twenty.
Our statistics professor was brilliant for most of that term. Clear notes, extra classes on Saturdays, jokes that actually worked. Then, in the last three weeks, his mother fell ill, and he came in tired, late, rushed. On feedback day I sat down and gave him two out of five for everything. "Disorganised," I wrote. I believed it completely.
Years later I found my old notebook from that course. Page after page of his neat examples, the Saturday sessions marked in red. I felt ashamed. I had judged a whole term by three weeks.
I, Uday, went up to him at a college reunion and told him so. He laughed and said my form was the only one he still remembered.

qa.a: Uday gave him two out of five for everything.

qa.q: Why did 'disorganised' feel true to Uday on feedback day?
qa.a: Uday felt frustrated by the rushed last three weeks, and that fresh memory seemed like the whole term.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed Uday's view, and why?
qa.a: Finding the old notebook full of neat examples and Saturday sessions showed the whole term, not just its end.

qa.q: How might the professor have felt reading the feedback?
qa.a: The professor may have felt hurt and discouraged, especially while his mother was ill, to see a term of effort rated two out of five.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a student course rating that gave too much weight to the last few weeks.

In the small meeting room of the city library, Charu opened the folder she had kept since January before Joseph's yearly review.
Joseph came in tense. The last month had been rough: he had mixed up two event dates, and a school group had turned up to a locked hall. He expected that to be the whole review.
"Let's go month by month," Charu said. She had a page for each. February: he set up the children's reading corner. April: he cleared the late-return backlog. July: three thank-you letters from readers. September: he helped train the new assistant. November: the date mix-up.
"I'd forgotten half of this," Joseph said.
"So had I, until I read my notes this morning," Charu admitted. "That's why I keep them."
They spent five minutes on November: what went wrong and what would help. The rest of the hour was about the other months.

qa.a: A page for each month means the whole year counts, so one bad November doesn't outweigh the reading corner or July's letters.

qa.a: Joseph goes from tense to relieved, seeing his whole year counted and not just the mix-up.

The magician was the best part. He pulled a pigeon out of Shalini's school bag, and the whole room screamed.

Shalini stared out at the rain. "It was ruined. The cake fell."

The school year had been Damini's best: new friends, first place in the science exhibition, a part in the play. Then came the last board paper, maths, in a hall with no fan on the hottest day of March. She blanked on two questions and walked out with a thumping head.
Two months later, on results day, she stood in a long queue in the heat outside the school office with Hrithik.
"This year was a disaster," she muttered.
"Disaster?" Hrithik said. "You won the exhibition. You were the best thing in the play."
"The last paper, though."
"Is one day. The year was two hundred days."
The queue shuffled forward. Damini tried to picture the exhibition, the applause, the play. They felt faded, far away. The hot hall felt like yesterday.
At the window she took her result slip. Maths: fine. Everything else: good. She laughed, a little shakily. "So it was a good year with a bad ending."

Saturday night.
Last shift at the bakery today. Two years, gone. And it ended with Kiran shouting at me over the cash drawer being short by two hundred rupees, in front of customers. I shouted back. I took off my apron and left without saying bye to anyone.
Right now, if you asked me, I'd say those two years were a waste. Worst job, worst boss.
But writing that, I have to be honest with this diary. Kiran gave me the job when I had no experience. Taught me to make croissants at 5 a.m. Covered my shifts when Nani was in hospital. Gave me a birthday cake with my name spelt wrong, which we laughed about for weeks.
Two years of that, and twenty minutes of shouting. Why are the twenty minutes the part I can see so clearly?
Maybe tomorrow I'll send Kiran a message. Not about the cash drawer. About the croissants.
Yash

Thursday.
The project review today could have been awful. Three months of late nights, the client changed everything twice, and Kishore and I had argued in front of the team last week. Everyone walked in tense.
I did the hard part in the middle: what went wrong, which calls were bad (including mine), what we'll change. Honest, not nice.
But I planned the last five minutes on purpose. I read out one specific thing each person did that saved us. For Kishore, the midnight fix in week six. Then I handed everyone a handwritten card and said, "Go home. Friday off."
Kishore stayed back and said, "That was the best ending to a bad project I've seen."
People remember the high point and the last bit. I can't fix the three months. I could choose the last five minutes.
Vandana

qa.a: Vandana read out one specific thing each person did that saved the project.
